solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Jolt in lifestyle, taking sect's wine across river

indicators.note: the sect's wine is laid across the river, so the river's letters sit within those words

parts.note: a cult is a sect, so the sect's is cult's
the Ure is a river in Yorkshire
hock is a German white wine

explanation.surface: A newcomer drinks the sect's communion wine on the far bank and finds their way of life upended.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taking' is only a link. The Ure is a river in the Yorkshire Dales, a crossword favourite.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names the disorientation felt on meeting an unfamiliar way of life, a jolt to one's lifestyle.

clue.text: Gossip's outstanding feature — wit

parts.note: the chin is a facial feature that juts out
a wag is a joker or wit

explanation.surface: Someone's most striking trait is their wit, says the gossip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'outstanding' means sticking out physically, not excellent.
explanation.definitionFit: Informal British word for a long friendly chat or natter, so a synonym of gossip as a noun.

clue.text: For example, a currency set up for animal accommodation

indicators.note: in a down clue, setting up lifts the letters so they read from bottom to top

parts.note: the rial is the currency of Iran and other countries

explanation.surface: Foreign money is put aside to build housing for livestock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'set up' reverses EG A RIAL in this down light.
explanation.definitionFit: A lairage is a place where cattle or sheep are rested on the way to market or slaughter.

clue.text: Improper distribution of lace in hut

indicators.note: the letters of the following words are spread out and redistributed

explanation.surface: Handing out lace in a hut sounds like a shady deal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'distribution of' rearranges LACE IN HUT.
explanation.definitionFit: Conduct that breaks moral or professional standards is improper, hence wrong in this ethical sense.

clue.text: Host's medal for gallantry mentioned in speech

indicators.note: said out loud, the two letters of the award sound like the word entered

parts.note: the MC is the Military Cross, a British award for gallantry

explanation.surface: The host's bravery medal gets a mention in an address.
explanation.walkthrough: The Military Cross (MC) is a British gallantry award; spoken, its two letters give the American spelling-out of master of ceremonies.
explanation.definitionFit: A master of ceremonies presents a show, so the presenter acts as host.

clue.text: He escaped maybe 45 minutes before policeman turned up at home

indicators.note: in a down clue the earlier piece is placed before the next one

parts.note: three quarters of an hour: three of the four letters of HOUR
DI is a detective inspector

indicators.note: in a down clue the letters are flipped to read upwards

parts.note: in means at home

explanation.surface: An escaped prisoner returns home 45 minutes ahead of the detective.
explanation.walkthrough: 45 minutes is three quarters of an hour, so take three of HOUR's four letters. 'turned up' reverses IN to NI.
explanation.definitionFit: Harry Houdini was the famous escapologist, an example of one who escaped, hence the question-like 'maybe'.

clue.text: Church artist capturing a chap's fantasy?

indicators.note: the church letters hold the chap inside them

parts.note: CE is the Church of England
a chap is him, a man referred to
RA is a Royal Academician, an artist

explanation.surface: A church painter holds a fellow in a picture of his imagination.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Church artist' reads as one painter, but splits into the Church of England and a Royal Academician.
explanation.definitionFit: A chimera is a wild, impossible imagining, and also a mythical monster; the question mark nods to that.

clue.text: Keep man in role of monarch without charge

parts.note: a keep is a castle stronghold, a fort
he is a man
as means in the role of
a king is a monarch

explanation.surface: A man is kept in the role of monarch without being charged.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Keep' is the noun, a castle tower, not the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Something available merely by requesting it costs nothing, so it is free of charge.

clue.text: Opening for Irishman initially involved with diamonds

indicators.note: involved means mixed up together, so these letters are jumbled
initially takes the first letter of the word that precedes it

parts.note: ice is slang for diamonds

explanation.surface: An Irishman gets mixed up in a diamond deal and sees an opening.
explanation.walkthrough: 'involved' jumbles the letters of 'for' with the Irishman's initial to give ORIF. 'Opening' sits at the front looking like a chance, but it means a hole.
explanation.definitionFit: An orifice is a hole or mouth in the body or an object, an opening.

clue.text: Formal warning demanding prudence

definitions.meaning: the official warning given by police before questioning or instead of charges

explanation.surface: An official warning that calls for prudence.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both a police warning and a quality of care, so both definitions fit.

clue.text: Cipher the setter possibly drinks in? Forget it!

parts.note: a cipher is a zero, nothing

indicators.note: drinks means takes in, so the dog swallows the next word

parts.note: a setter is a breed of dog, so a dog generally

explanation.surface: A nobody wonders whether the setter of the puzzle drinks in a pub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the setter' looks like the crossword's compiler; it is the gun dog, which 'drinks' the word in.
explanation.definitionFit: A colloquial refusal, meaning there is no chance, equivalent to forget it.

clue.text: Wife wearing top hat, oddly, for walk by river

indicators.note: the jumbled hat is worn by the wife, so it goes round her letter
oddly means arranged strangely, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A wife in a strangely worn top hat strolls by the river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'oddly' rearranges TOP HAT as TOPATH, and 'wearing' places W inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A path beside a river or canal used originally by horses hauling boats, so a riverside walk.

clue.text: Renowned English medic primarily concerned with otolaryngology

indicators.note: primarily takes the opening letter of the word before it

parts.note: in means involved or concerned with
ENT is ear, nose and throat, the hospital term for this specialty

explanation.surface: A famous English doctor specialises in ear, nose and throat surgery.
explanation.walkthrough: ENT (ear, nose and throat) is the everyday name for otolaryngology.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone distinguished and well known in their field is renowned.

clue.text: Bore raring to be heard

indicators.note: the word for raring is spoken and its sound gives the entry

parts.note: raring to go means eager

explanation.surface: Someone tedious is desperate to get a hearing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bore' looks like a tedious person; it is a tidal bore, a wave surging up a river such as the Severn or Trent.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is a dialect name for a tidal wave rushing up an estuary, a bore.

clue.text: Hubbub exposed in daily, one modified when editor's absent

parts.note: a daily is a cleaning woman, a char
one is the Roman numeral I

indicators.note: absent signals that the editor's letters are taken away

parts.note: varied means changed or modified
ED is short for editor

explanation.surface: A rumpus breaks out in a daily paper when one story is changed with the editor away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'daily' is a British cleaning lady (char), not a newspaper.
explanation.definitionFit: A charivari is a noisy mock serenade, by extension any cacophonous din or uproar.

clue.text: Reportedly throw out church carpet

indicators.note: the word for throw out is spoken, its sound giving the first piece

parts.note: to axe is to dismiss or discard
a minster is a large church, as in York Minster

explanation.surface: Rumour has it a church's carpet is being thrown out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reportedly' turns AXE into its homophone AX.
explanation.definitionFit: A type of tufted carpet named after the Devon town where it was first woven.

clue.text: Misusing a mug, slurp something sweet

indicators.note: misusing the letters means putting them to the wrong order

explanation.surface: Someone drinks noisily from a mug, slurping a sweet treat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Misusing' rearranges A MUG SLURP.
explanation.definitionFit: A small round sweet, a candy, so something sweet.

clue.text: Old-fashioned resentment when leader goes for good fish

indicators.note: goes for means is replaced by, so the opening letter is swapped

parts.note: dudgeon is a dated word for indignant resentment
the leader is the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: An old grudge flares when a leader leaves a fine fish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leader' is the first letter of DUDGEON, which G replaces.
explanation.definitionFit: A gudgeon is a small freshwater fish of the carp family.

clue.text: Rest in park next to bar

parts.note: a rec is a recreation ground, a public park
a bar is a stripe or line

explanation.surface: Relax in the park next to a pub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bar' looks like a pub; it is a line. REC (recreation ground) is British for a park.
explanation.definitionFit: To recline is to lean back and relax, so it means rest as a verb.

clue.text: Changing sides, fetch flashy jewellery

indicators.note: right is switched for left, the two side letters

parts.note: to fetch is to bring

explanation.surface: A turncoat is told to fetch gaudy jewels.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Changing sides' swaps R (right) for L (left).
explanation.definitionFit: Slang for showy, ostentatious jewellery, so flashy jewellery.

clue.text: Town crier's ringer going over island

indicators.note: in a down clue going over places the first piece above the second

parts.note: a bell is a thing that rings
the Isle of Man is an island

explanation.surface: A town crier rings his bell on a trip over to an island.
explanation.walkthrough: MAN is the Isle of Man, in the Irish Sea.
explanation.definitionFit: A bellman rang a handbell to announce public news, so he was a town crier.

clue.text: Engross tail end of form in this writer's language

indicators.note: the final letter is placed in the middle of the words that follow

parts.note: this writer is the setter, so this writer's means I am, IM
Erse is Irish Gaelic, a language

indicators.note: the tail end is the last letter of the word that follows

explanation.surface: The tail of a form is written in the setter's own language.
explanation.walkthrough: 'this writer's' is the setter saying 'I'm'; Erse is Irish Gaelic. 'in' places the final M of form between them.
explanation.definitionFit: To immerse someone is to absorb them deeply in something, engrossing them.

clue.text: Takes risks with popular exponents

parts.note: in means fashionable or popular
dices, as in dices with death, means takes risks

explanation.surface: A popular gambler takes risks with promoters of causes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'exponents' looks like advocates; it is the mathematical sense, powers.
explanation.definitionFit: In algebra the small raised numbers showing a power are exponents, and the plural of index names them.

clue.text: Dawn's lad on telephone at university

indicators.note: on the phone the word is heard, not seen, so it is its homophone

parts.note: a son is a lad
up means at university, as in up at Oxford

explanation.surface: Dawn's son phones from university.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dawn' looks like a woman's name. UP is a British usage: students go up to university.
explanation.definitionFit: The moment the sun rises is daybreak, which is dawn.

clue.text: Fellow backing judge leaving large aircraft plant

indicators.note: backing means going backwards, so the name is read in reverse

parts.note: Len is a man's name, any fellow

indicators.note: leaving means the judge's letter departs from the aircraft

parts.note: a jumbo is a jumbo jet

explanation.surface: A man supports a judge who leaves a jumbo jet in a factory.
explanation.walkthrough: 'plant' looks like a factory; it is the lotus genus, an obscure word. 'backing' reverses LEN.
explanation.definitionFit: Nelumbo is the genus of the lotus, a water plant.

clue.text: Classically simple part of City toured by old lady

indicators.note: the old lady travels around the district, so her letters surround it

parts.note: gran is a grandmother, an old lady
EC1 is a London postal district in the City, with 1 as the numeral I

explanation.surface: A granny gives a tour of a plain corner of the City of London.
explanation.walkthrough: EC1 is a London postcode around the City, the financial district; the 1 becomes I.
explanation.definitionFit: Grecian describes the plain elegant style of ancient Greek art, so classically simple.

clue.text: Monkey, yellow-brown, seen around first day of month

indicators.note: the colour goes around the date, enclosing it

parts.note: tan is a yellowish-brown colour
Mar 1 is the first of March, with 1 as I

explanation.surface: A tawny monkey is spotted at the start of the month.
explanation.walkthrough: 'first day of month' gives MAR I, the 1st of March, with the numeral as I.
explanation.definitionFit: A tamarin is a small South American monkey.

clue.text: Fuming, one arrests any number for excessive drinking

parts.note: someone fuming is in a temper

indicators.note: arrests means holds, so the number is held inside

parts.note: an ace is a one in cards or dice
N stands for any number in algebra

explanation.surface: A furious person locks up a crowd for heavy drinking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'arrests' puts N inside ACE, giving ANCE after IN TEMPER.
explanation.definitionFit: Intemperance is lack of moderation, used especially of overindulgence in alcohol.
